Foraging ecology in the European white stork is intimately tied to open agricultural landscapes and ephemeral wetlands, where individuals employ a tactile foraging strategy to capture a diverse array of prey. The species' habit of following agricultural machinery to capture disturbed invertebrates is a well-documented behavioural adaptation that buffers against local declines in natural prey density. During migration, which follows either the western route via Gibraltar or the eastern route through the Bosporus, storks rely heavily on thermal soaring to minimise energetic expenditure, a flight mode that requires stable atmospheric conditions and imposes constraints on crossing large water bodies. Juvenile birds, upon attaining nutritional independence after the post-fledging dispersal phase, must rapidly develop proficient foraging skills to sustain their substantial daily energy requirements during their first southward migration.
